questions.q: a and b are real, a > 0, and (a + bi)² = −7 − 24i. What is b?
questions.x: a² − b² = −7 and 2ab = −24, so b = −12/a and a⁴ + 7a² − 144 = 0, giving a² = 9, a = 3 and b = −4. Check: (3 − 4i)² = 9 − 24i − 16 = −7 − 24i. The sign of b must match the sign of 2ab = −24.
A − B keeps the elements of A that are not in B: removing 2 and 4 leaves {1, 3, 5}. {6} is B − A, {2, 4} is A ∩ B and {1, 3, 5, 6} is the symmetric difference.

questions.q: A town's population doubles every 15 years. It is 50,000 now. What will it be after 60 years if this continues?
questions.x: 60 years is 60/15 = 4 doubling periods, so the population becomes 50,000 × 2⁴ = 50,000 × 16 = 800,000. Multiplying by 4, the number of periods, gives 200,000.

questions.q: Which function can be made continuous at x = 0 by suitably defining its value f(0)?
questions.x: (sin x)/x → 1 as x → 0, so defining f(0) = 1 makes it continuous (a removable discontinuity). 1/x and 1/x² grow without bound, and |x|/x has left limit −1 and right limit 1, so no value of f(0) helps.

questions.q: What is the determinant of the matrix [[i, 1], [1, i]], where i² = −1?
questions.x: |[[i, 1], [1, i]]| = i·i − 1·1 = −1 − 1 = −2. Using i² = 1 by mistake gives 0.

questions.q: Every entry in one row of a square matrix is zero. What is its determinant?
o: it cannot be found without the other entries
questions.x: Expand the determinant along the zero row: every term has a factor 0, so the determinant is 0 whatever the other entries are.

questions.q: What is the range of f(x) = −2x² + 4x + 1, where x is any real number?
questions.x: f(x) = −2(x² − 2x) + 1 = −2(x − 1)² + 2 + 1 = 3 − 2(x − 1)². The leading coefficient is negative, so the parabola opens downward and the range is y ≤ 3. Check: f(1) = −2 + 4 + 1 = 3.

questions.q: If (ax + b)/((x − 1)(x − 2)) = 3/(x − 2) − 1/(x − 1) for all suitable x, what are a and b?
questions.x: Combine the right side: 3(x − 1) − (x − 2) = 3x − 3 − x + 2 = 2x − 1, so a = 2 and b = −1. Check at x = 0: (−1)/2 = −3/2 + 1 = −1/2. Adding the two fractions instead of subtracting gives 4x − 5.

questions.q: What is the value of Σ (2k + 1) for k = 1 to 10?
questions.x: Σ(2k + 1) = 2Σk + Σ1 = 2 × 55 + 10 = 120. Check: the terms are 3, 5, …, 21, and 10 × (3 + 21)/2 = 120. Forgetting the +1 in every term gives 110.

questions.q: A leap year is chosen at random. What is the probability that it has 53 Fridays?
questions.x: 366 days = 52 weeks + 2 days, so there are 52 Fridays plus the 2 extra consecutive days. Of the 7 equally likely pairs (Sun-Mon, …, Sat-Sun), Thu-Fri and Fri-Sat contain a Friday: 2/7. A normal year with 1 extra day would give 1/7.

questions.q: A committee of 4 is chosen from 5 married couples so that no husband and wife are both on it. In how many ways can this be done?
questions.x: First choose which 4 of the 5 couples are represented: C(5, 4) = 5. Then pick husband or wife from each: 2⁴ = 16. Total 5 × 16 = 80. Check: of the C(10, 4) = 210 committees, 130 contain at least one couple.

questions.q: In the expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ, the coefficient of x² is 4 times the coefficient of x. What is n?
questions.x: ⁿC₂ / ⁿC₁ = [n(n − 1)/2]/n = (n − 1)/2 = 4, so n = 9. Check: ⁹C₂ = 36 = 4 × 9. Forgetting the 2 in ⁿC₂ gives n = 5.

questions.q: What is each interior angle of a regular hexagon in radians?
questions.x: The interior angles of a hexagon add to (6 − 2) × 180° = 720°, so each is 120° = 2π/3. π/3 is the exterior angle.

questions.q: What is the value of cos 15° − sin 15°?
questions.x: sin 15° = cos 75°, so cos 15° − cos 75° = −2 sin 45° sin(−30°) = 2 × √2/2 × 1/2 = √2/2. Check by squaring: 1 − 2 sin 15° cos 15° = 1 − sin 30° = 1/2. √6/2 is cos 15° + sin 15°.

questions.q: For 0 ≤ x < 2π, at which x does y = 3 − 2 sin x take its greatest value?
questions.x: y is greatest when sin x is least, sin x = −1, at x = 3π/2, giving y = 5. At x = π/2 the value is 1, the least value.

questions.q: In triangle ABC with inradius r and s = (a + b + c)/2, which relation is correct?
questions.x: The tangents from vertex A to the incircle have length s − a, and the radius makes a right angle with each, so r = (s − a) tan(A/2). s tan(A/2) is r₁, the escribed radius opposite A.

questions.q: The value of cos⁻¹(−√3/2) − sin⁻¹(−1/2) is:
questions.x: cos⁻¹(−√3/2) = π − π/6 = 5π/6 and sin⁻¹(−1/2) = −π/6, so the difference is 5π/6 + π/6 = π. Dropping the minus sign of sin⁻¹(−1/2) gives 2π/3.

questions.q: The general solution of 2 cos²θ + 5 sin θ − 4 = 0 is (n ∈ Z):
questions.x: Replace cos²θ by 1 − sin²θ: 2 sin²θ − 5 sin θ + 2 = 0, i.e. (2 sin θ − 1)(sin θ − 2) = 0. sin θ = 2 is impossible, so sin θ = 1/2 and θ = nπ + (−1)ⁿ π/6. Check π/6: 2(3/4) + 5/2 − 4 = 0.

questions.q: What is the slope of the normal to the curve y = x² at the point (1, 1)?
questions.x: The tangent slope is y′ = 2x = 2 at x = 1, and the normal is perpendicular to it, so its slope is −1/2. The value 2 is the tangent slope.

questions.q: For −1 < x < 1, what is d/dx (sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x)?
questions.x: The derivatives are 1/√(1 − x²) and −1/√(1 − x²), which cancel. This agrees with sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2, a constant; π/2 is the value of the sum, not its derivative.

questions.q: Using u = √x, ∫ e^(√x)/√x dx, for x > 0, equals:
questions.x: u = √x gives du = dx/(2√x), so dx/√x = 2 du and the integral is 2∫eᵘ du = 2e^(√x) + C. Check: d/dx 2e^(√x) = 2e^(√x)/(2√x).

questions.q: Using u = x² + 1, ∫₀¹ x/(x² + 1)² dx equals:
questions.x: du = 2x dx and the limits become u = 1 to u = 2: ½∫₁² u⁻² du = ½[−1/u]₁² = ½(1 − ½) = 1/4. Leaving out the factor ½ gives 1/2.

questions.q: What is the general solution of dy/dx = eˣ·y²?
questions.x: Separate: dy/y² = eˣ dx, so −1/y = eˣ + k, i.e. 1/y + eˣ = c. Check: differentiating gives −y′/y² + eˣ = 0, so y′ = eˣy².

questions.q: What is the circumcentre of the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 4)?
questions.x: The angle at the origin is 90°, so the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse from (6, 0) to (0, 4): (3, 2). Check: it is √13 from each vertex. (2, 4/3) is the centroid.

questions.q: The midpoints of the sides of a triangle are (1, 2), (3, 4) and (5, 0). What is the centroid of the triangle?
questions.x: The triangle of midpoints has the same centroid as the original: ((1 + 3 + 5)/3, (2 + 4 + 0)/3) = (3, 2). Check: the vertices are (−1, 6), (7, 2) and (3, −2), whose centroid is also (3, 2).

questions.q: The point (k, 2) lies in the region 3x − y < 4. What are the possible values of k?
questions.x: Substitute: 3k − 2 < 4 gives 3k < 6, so k < 2. Check k = 0: −2 < 4 is true.

questions.q: Which circle is concentric with x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 3 = 0 and passes through (1, 1)?
questions.x: Same centre means x² + y² − 4x + 6y + c = 0. Through (1, 1): 1 + 1 − 4 + 6 + c = 0, so c = −4. Check: centre (2, −3), r² = 4 + 9 + 4 = 17 = (1 − 2)² + (1 + 3)².

questions.q: A force of 10 N acts in the direction of 3i + 4j and moves a particle from the origin to the point (2, 1), distances in metres. What is the work done?
questions.x: F = 10(3i + 4j)/5 = 6i + 8j, so W = F · d = 6 × 2 + 8 × 1 = 20 J. Using 3i + 4j itself as the force gives 10 J.

questions.q: A particle moves with position r(t) = eᵗ cos t i + eᵗ sin t j. What is its speed at time t?
questions.x: v = eᵗ(cos t − sin t)i + eᵗ(sin t + cos t)j, and |v|² = e^(2t)[(cos t − sin t)² + (sin t + cos t)²] = 2e^(2t). So the speed is √2 eᵗ. Forgetting the product rule gives eᵗ.

questions.q: A particle has velocity v = t² − 4t + 3 m/s. What is its speed at t = 2 s?
questions.x: v(2) = 4 − 8 + 3 = −1 m/s, so it is moving backwards with speed |−1| = 1 m/s. Speed is the size of the velocity and is never negative.

questions.q: The period of a pendulum is calculated from T = 2π√(l/g), with g taken as exact. If the length l is measured with a 4 % uncertainty, the percentage uncertainty in T is:
questions.x: T ∝ l^½, so the percentage uncertainty in T is ½ × 4 % = 2 %. Copying the 4 % unchanged, or doubling it to 8 % as for a square, are the usual slips.

questions.q: A couple consists of two equal and opposite parallel forces of 10 N each, whose lines of action are 0.3 m apart. The torque of the couple is:
questions.x: Torque of a couple = one force × perpendicular distance between the lines of action = 10 × 0.3 = 3 N m. Zero is tempting because the net force is zero, but the torques add. 6 N m counts both forces at the full 0.3 m.

questions.q: Which of these collisions is very nearly elastic?
o: A bullet embedding itself in a wooden block
A collision between two molecules of an ideal gas
A lump of wet clay hitting the floor
questions.x: In an elastic collision kinetic energy is conserved; collisions of ideal-gas molecules are treated as perfectly elastic. In the others the bodies stick or deform, so kinetic energy is lost and the collisions are inelastic.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 30 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its height above the point of projection 4 s later is:
questions.x: s = ut − ½gt² = 30 × 4 − 5 × 16 = 120 − 80 = 40 m. Check: it reaches 45 m at 3 s and falls 5 m in the next second. 50 m is the total distance travelled (45 + 5), not the height.

questions.q: The ratio of the escape velocity from the Earth's surface to the speed of a satellite in a circular orbit just above the surface is:
questions.x: Escape velocity = √(2gR) and orbital speed close to the surface = √(gR), so the ratio is √2. Forgetting the square root gives 2; inverting the ratio gives 1/√2.

questions.q: The minute hand and the hour hand of a clock both turn steadily. The ratio of the angular velocity of the minute hand to that of the hour hand is:
questions.x: The minute hand makes one revolution in 1 h and the hour hand in 12 h. Since ω = 2π/T, the ratio is 12 : 1. Putting the periods the wrong way round gives 1 : 12.

questions.q: Satellite P orbits a planet in a circular orbit of radius r with period T. Satellite Q orbits the same planet in a circular orbit of radius 9r. The period of Q is:
questions.x: v = √(GM/r), so T = 2πr/v = 2π√(r³/GM) and T ∝ r^(3/2): 9^(3/2) = 27, so Q's period is 27T (check: Q's speed is v/3 over a path 9 times as long, 9 × 3 = 27). Using T ∝ √r gives 3T; T ∝ r gives 9T.

questions.q: A body floats at rest, partly submerged in a liquid. The upthrust on it is:
questions.x: The body is in equilibrium, so the upward upthrust balances its weight exactly (law of flotation). If the upthrust were greater it would rise; if less it would sink.

questions.q: The suspension of a car has a natural frequency of 1.5 Hz. The car is driven along a road with small ridges evenly spaced 6 m apart. Its bouncing is greatest at a speed of:
questions.x: The ridges drive the suspension at f = v/d. Resonance when v/6 = 1.5, so v = 9 m s⁻¹ (check: one ridge every 6/9 s = 0.67 s, the natural period). Dividing 6 by 1.5 gives 4 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A source of sound moves steadily towards a stationary observer in still air. Compared with when the source is at rest, the sound reaching the observer has:
o: A shorter wavelength and a greater speed
A longer wavelength and the same speed
The same wavelength and a greater speed
A shorter wavelength and the same speed
questions.x: The speed of sound is set by the air, not by the source, so it is unchanged. The moving source crowds the waves together in front of it, so the wavelength is shorter and the frequency higher.

questions.q: In a stationary wave of wavelength λ, the distance between a node and the next antinode is:
questions.x: Neighbouring nodes are λ/2 apart, and an antinode lies midway between them, so node to next antinode is λ/4. λ/2 is the node-to-node distance.

questions.q: Huygens' construction is applied to a plane wavefront that is reflected from a plane mirror. It shows that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence because:
o: The secondary wavelets travel back through the same medium at the same speed as the incident wave
The wavelets slow down after reflection
The frequency of the light doubles on reflection
The mirror absorbs half of each wavelet
questions.x: In the time the edge of the incident wavefront reaches the mirror, the wavelets from the points already reflected grow by the same distance, because the speed is unchanged in the same medium. The two right-angled triangles in the construction are then congruent, so the angles are equal.

questions.q: The same convex lens is used as a magnifying glass by the same person, once with the final image at the near point and once with the final image at infinity. The magnifying power at the near point is greater by:
questions.x: With the image at the near point M = 1 + d/f, and with the image at infinity M = d/f. The difference is exactly 1, whatever the focal length.

questions.q: Entropy is a measure of the:
o: Total heat contained in a system
questions.x: Entropy measures the disorder (randomness) of a system; a change in it for a reversible process is ΔS = ΔQ/T. It is not the same as heat or temperature.

questions.q: A rigid cylinder holds an ideal gas at 27 °C and 6 × 10⁵ Pa. Some gas is let out, and the gas left inside is then warmed to 127 °C, when its pressure is 4 × 10⁵ Pa. What fraction of the original mass of gas remains?
questions.x: For fixed volume, n ∝ p/T: before 6 × 10⁵/300 = 2000, after 4 × 10⁵/400 = 1000, so half the gas remains. Ignoring the temperature change gives 2/3.

questions.q: Four charges of +2 nC each are placed at the corners of a square. Each corner is 10 cm from the centre of the square. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the potential and the electric field at the centre are:
questions.x: Potentials add as scalars: V = 4 × 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁹/0.1 = 4 × 180 = 720 V. The four field vectors cancel in opposite pairs by symmetry, so E = 0. 180 V is one charge only.

questions.q: In an inkjet printer, an ink drop of mass 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ kg carries a charge of 2 × 10⁻¹³ C. It moves at 20 m s⁻¹ between deflecting plates 1 cm long, where a uniform field of 1 × 10⁶ N C⁻¹ acts across its path. Ignoring gravity, how far is it deflected sideways while between the plates?
questions.x: a = qE/m = 2 × 10⁻¹³ × 10⁶/10⁻¹⁰ = 2 × 10³ m s⁻². Time between plates t = 0.01/20 = 5 × 10⁻⁴ s. Deflection y = ½at² = ½ × 2 × 10³ × 2.5 × 10⁻⁷ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.25 mm. Forgetting the ½ gives 0.5 mm.

questions.q: A carbon resistor (temperature coefficient −5 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹) is connected in series with an iron wire (temperature coefficient +5 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹). Their total resistance is 110 Ω and, for small temperature changes, does not change with temperature. The resistance of the carbon resistor is:
questions.x: For no net change, the rise in the iron's resistance must cancel the fall in the carbon's: R(carbon) × 5 × 10⁻⁴ = R(iron) × 5 × 10⁻³, so R(carbon) = 10 R(iron). Then 11 R(iron) = 110 Ω gives R(iron) = 10 Ω and R(carbon) = 100 Ω. Swapping the two gives 10 Ω.

questions.q: When a Wheatstone bridge is balanced, the two points joined by the galvanometer are:
o: At different potentials, so a large current flows through the galvanometer
At the same potential, so no current flows through the galvanometer
Joined directly to the positive terminal of the battery
At zero potential only when the battery is removed
questions.x: Balance means zero galvanometer current, which happens only when there is no p.d. between its two ends: the two junctions are at equal potentials.

questions.q: A straight current-carrying wire at 30° to a uniform magnetic field experiences a force F. The wire is turned until it is at 90° to the field, with the same current. The force on it becomes:
questions.x: F = BIL sin θ, so the force goes from BIL × 0.5 to BIL × 1: it doubles to 2F. Using cos instead of sin would give a smaller force.

questions.q: The output of a simple DC generator with a single coil and a split-ring commutator is:
o: Perfectly steady, like that of a battery
Zero on average over a complete turn
In one direction, but rising from zero to a maximum and back twice every turn
questions.x: The commutator only reverses the connections; the coil's emf still varies as sin ωt, so the output is the rectified shape |sin ωt|: one direction but pulsating, with two peaks per revolution.

questions.q: A coil connected to a 10 V DC supply draws 2 A. Connected to a 10 V rms AC supply, it draws 1 A rms. The inductive reactance of the coil at the AC frequency is:
questions.x: On DC only resistance acts: R = 10/2 = 5 Ω. On AC the impedance is Z = 10/1 = 10 Ω, and Z² = R² + XL², so XL = √(100 − 25) = √75 = 5√3 Ω (about 8.7 Ω). Taking XL = Z − R gives 5 Ω; taking it as Z gives 10 Ω.

questions.q: Wires P and Q have the same length and the same cross-sectional area. They are joined end to end and hang vertically with a load at the bottom. The Young's modulus of P is twice that of Q. The total extension is 3 mm. The extension of P is:
questions.x: Both wires carry the same tension, so extension e = FL/(AY) is proportional to 1/Y: e_P = ½e_Q. Then e_P + 2e_P = 3 mm gives e_P = 1 mm (and e_Q = 2 mm). Giving the stiffer wire the larger share gives 2 mm; sharing equally gives 1.5 mm.

questions.q: Inputs P and Q are fed to an AND gate, and its output is passed through a NOT gate. The final output is 0 for:
o: P = 1, Q = 0 and P = 0, Q = 1 only
Every combination of P and Q
questions.x: The final output is NOT(P·Q), the NAND function. P·Q = 1 only when both inputs are 1, so the final output is 0 only for P = 1, Q = 1. P = 0, Q = 0 is the only zero of an OR gate, not of this circuit.

questions.q: A torch bulb, an ideal diode and a battery are connected in series. The bulb glows. The battery is now turned round, with nothing else changed. The bulb:
o: Does not glow, because the diode is now reverse biased
questions.x: Reversing the battery reverse biases the diode, which then allows almost no current, so the bulb goes out. A diode conducts in one direction only; alternate half-cycles would need an AC supply.

questions.q: The temperature of a black body is raised. The wavelength at which it emits radiation with maximum intensity:
questions.x: By Wien's displacement law λ_max T = constant, so a higher temperature gives a shorter λ_max. This is why a heated iron rod glows dull red first and then orange, yellow and white as it gets hotter.

questions.q: In an X-ray tube the target metal is changed to a different element, while the accelerating voltage is kept the same. Which change takes place in the X-ray spectrum?
o: The characteristic lines move to new wavelengths, but the shortest (cut-off) wavelength stays the same
The cut-off wavelength changes, but the characteristic lines stay the same
Both the characteristic lines and the cut-off wavelength stay the same
The spectrum becomes a single characteristic line
questions.x: Characteristic lines come from electron jumps between inner shells of the target atoms, so they depend on the element. The cut-off wavelength λmin = hc/eV depends only on the accelerating voltage V.

questions.q: A sample contains 5 × 10¹⁵ radioactive nuclei of a nuclide with half-life 693 s. Using λ = 0.693/T½, the activity of the sample is:
questions.x: λ = 0.693/693 = 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹, so A = λN = 10⁻³ × 5 × 10¹⁵ = 5 × 10¹² Bq. Dividing N by T½ without the 0.693 gives 7.2 × 10¹² Bq; multiplying N by 0.693 alone gives 3.5 × 10¹⁵ Bq.

questions.q: A meson contains a strange quark (charge −⅓e) together with one antiquark, and its total charge is −e. The meson's quark content is:
questions.x: A meson is one quark plus one antiquark. s (−⅓e) + ū (−⅔e) = −1e. s d̄ gives −⅓ + ⅓ = 0; s̄ u contains an antistrange quark and gives +1e; s u is two quarks, not a quark-antiquark pair.

questions.q: The luminosity of a star is:
o: The power received per square metre at the Earth
The total power it radiates in all directions
questions.x: Luminosity L is the total energy a star radiates per second, measured in watts. The power received per square metre at a distance d is the radiant flux F = L/(4πd²), which depends on distance as well.

questions.q: What mass of sulphur dioxide, SO₂, contains the same number of oxygen atoms as 8.8 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂? (C = 12, O = 16, S = 32)
questions.x: 8.8 g CO₂ = 8.8/44 = 0.2 mol, holding 0.4 mol O atoms. SO₂ also has 2 O per molecule, so 0.2 mol SO₂ is needed = 0.2 × 64 = 12.8 g. Taking equal masses gives 8.8 g, and halving or doubling the mole ratio by mistake gives 6.4 g or 25.6 g.

questions.q: How many gas molecules are present in 1 cm³ of an ideal gas at STP? (Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³)
questions.x: 22.4 dm³ = 22 400 cm³ holds 6.02 × 10²³ molecules, so 1 cm³ holds 6.02 × 10²³/22 400 = 2.69 × 10¹⁹. 2.69 × 10²² is the number per dm³ (cm³ not converted).

questions.q: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain:
questions.x: Avogadro's law is about the number of molecules (moles). Equal numbers of atoms is wrong because molecules such as He, O₂ and O₃ have different numbers of atoms; masses and densities depend on the molar mass.

questions.q: A unit cell has a = b ≠ c and α = β = γ = 90°. It belongs to the:
questions.x: Two equal edges with all angles 90° is tetragonal. Cubic needs all three edges equal, orthorhombic has all three different, and hexagonal has one angle of 120°.

questions.q: Which arrangement breaks the Pauli exclusion principle?
o: Two electrons in the same 2s orbital, with opposite spins
One electron in each of the 2pₓ and 2pᵧ orbitals, with parallel spins
The 2s orbital filled before any 2p orbital
Two electrons in the same 2s orbital, both with spin +½
questions.x: Two electrons in one orbital already share n, l and m, so they must differ in spin; both +½ gives identical sets of four quantum numbers. Parallel spins in different p orbitals follow Hund's rule and are allowed.

questions.q: On moving down a group of the periodic table, the first ionisation energy generally decreases. The main reason is that:
o: The nuclear charge decreases down the group
The number of valence electrons decreases down the group
The atomic radius and the shielding by inner electrons increase, so the outer electron is held less firmly
The outer electron moves into a lower energy level
questions.x: Down a group each element has one more shell, so the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and better shielded; this outweighs the larger nuclear charge. The nuclear charge actually increases, and the number of valence electrons stays the same within a group.

questions.q: A bomb calorimeter is calibrated: a reaction known to release 3.30 kJ raises its temperature by 1.50 K. Then 0.010 mol of a fuel burnt in the same calorimeter raises the temperature by 2.00 K. What is ΔE of combustion of the fuel?
questions.x: Heat capacity of the calorimeter = 3.30 ÷ 1.50 = 2.20 kJ K⁻¹. Heat from the fuel = 2.20 × 2.00 = 4.40 kJ, so ΔE = −4.40 ÷ 0.010 = −440 kJ mol⁻¹. −4.40 forgets to divide by the moles; −91 comes from inverting the heat capacity (1.50 ÷ 3.30).

questions.q: In a bomb calorimeter, the substance under test is burnt:
o: In an open glass beaker in air, at constant pressure
In a sealed vessel from which all air has been removed
In a sealed steel vessel containing oxygen under pressure, at constant volume
In a flame under a beaker of water open to the air
questions.x: The bomb is a strong steel vessel filled with oxygen under pressure and sealed, so combustion is complete and happens at constant volume; it stands in a known mass of water. The open beaker or flame describes simpler calorimeters, which work at constant pressure.

questions.q: For a reversible reaction started with reactants only, graphs of concentration against time are drawn for a reactant and a product. Once equilibrium is reached, the two curves:
o: Both become horizontal, usually at different concentrations
Become horizontal at the same concentration
questions.x: At equilibrium the concentrations no longer change, so each curve levels off; the levels are generally different, set by the value of K. The rate–time curves for forward and reverse reactions do meet, which is why 'same concentration' is tempting.

questions.q: A solution contains 0.10 mol dm⁻³ Mg²⁺ ions. Ksp of Mg(OH)₂ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ at 25 °C. At what pH does Mg(OH)₂ just begin to precipitate as NaOH is slowly added? (Kw = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴)
questions.x: Precipitation starts when [Mg²⁺][OH⁻]² = Ksp: [OH⁻]² = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ ÷ 0.10 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰, so [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵, pOH = 5.0 and pH = 9.0. 5.0 is the pOH; 8.5 comes from ignoring the 0.10 mol dm⁻³ of Mg²⁺ and taking [OH⁻] = √Ksp.

questions.q: Aluminium sulphate, Al₂(SO₄)₃, is fully dissociated in a 0.10 mol dm⁻³ aqueous solution. What is the concentration of sulphate ions?
questions.x: Al₂(SO₄)₃ → 2Al³⁺ + 3SO₄²⁻, so [SO₄²⁻] = 3 × 0.10 = 0.30 mol dm⁻³. 0.20 mol dm⁻³ is the Al³⁺ concentration and 0.50 mol dm⁻³ is the total of all ions.

questions.q: In the reaction 2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S + 2H₂O, which species is the oxidising agent?
questions.x: Sulphur in SO₂ goes from +4 to 0, so SO₂ is reduced and is the oxidising agent. Sulphur in H₂S goes from −2 to 0; H₂S is oxidised and is the reducing agent, the usual mix-up.

questions.q: For a reaction, rate = k[X][Y]². If [X] is halved and [Y] is tripled at the same temperature, the rate becomes:
questions.x: New rate ∝ (1/2) × 3² = 9/2 = 4.5 times. Forgetting to square the [Y] factor gives 1.5; ignoring the halving of [X] gives 9.

questions.q: For magnesium, the enthalpy of atomisation is +148 kJ mol⁻¹, the first ionisation energy is 738 kJ mol⁻¹ and the second ionisation energy is 1451 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the energy needed for Mg(s) → Mg²⁺(g) + 2e⁻?
questions.x: Mg(s) → Mg(g) needs 148 kJ, then both ionisation energies: 148 + 738 + 1451 = 2337 kJ mol⁻¹. Ionisation energies refer to gaseous atoms, so leaving out the atomisation step gives 2189 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: Which element is a metalloid?
questions.x: Silicon has properties between metals and non-metals (for example it is a semiconductor), so it is a metalloid. Magnesium and aluminium are metals; phosphorus is a non-metal.

questions.q: 6.2 g of boric acid, H₃BO₃, is titrated with 1.0 mol dm⁻³ NaOH, glycerol being added to sharpen the end point. What volume of NaOH is needed? (H = 1, B = 11, O = 16)
questions.x: M(H₃BO₃) = 3 + 11 + 48 = 62 g mol⁻¹, so 6.2 g = 0.10 mol. Boric acid is monobasic (it accepts OH⁻ to give [B(OH)₄]⁻), so 0.10 mol NaOH = 100 cm³. Treating it as tribasic because it has three H atoms gives 300 cm³.

questions.q: Ammonia is prepared in the laboratory: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O. What volume of ammonia at STP is obtained from 10.7 g of NH₄Cl? (N = 14, H = 1, Cl = 35.5; molar volume 22.4 dm³)
questions.x: M(NH₄Cl) = 53.5 g mol⁻¹, so 10.7 g = 0.20 mol; NH₄Cl and NH₃ are 2 : 2, so 0.20 mol NH₃ = 0.20 × 22.4 = 4.48 dm³. Halving the moles as if 2 mol NH₄Cl gave 1 mol NH₃ gives 2.24 dm³.

questions.q: Dilute sulphuric acid is added to bleaching powder. The gas given off is:
questions.x: Ca(OCl)Cl + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + Cl₂ + H₂O: the OCl⁻ (Cl +1) and Cl⁻ (Cl −1) combine to give Cl₂ (0). Atom check: Ca, S, 2 Cl, 2 H and 5 O balance on both sides. Thinking the acid simply displaces HCl is the slip.

questions.q: Small atoms such as H, C and N can fit into the spaces of a transition metal lattice. The interstitial compounds formed, such as steel and TiC, are usually:
o: Softer than the pure metal and strictly stoichiometric
Harder than the pure metal and non-stoichiometric
questions.x: The small atoms in the holes stop the metal layers sliding, so the material becomes harder and more brittle, and the amount taken up varies, so the formula is often non-stoichiometric. The ionic option is wrong because the metallic lattice remains.

questions.q: Which pair are chain isomers?
questions.x: Butane and 2-methylpropane have the same formula C₄H₁₀ but different carbon skeletons (straight and branched), so they are chain isomers. Ethanol/methoxymethane and propanal/propanone are functional group isomers, and but-2-ene/but-1-ene are position isomers.

questions.q: The reactivity of the hydrogen halides in electrophilic addition to an alkene follows the order:
questions.x: The H–X bond gets weaker from HCl to HI, so HI gives up H⁺ to the π bond most easily. Choosing HCl first confuses bond polarity with bond strength.

questions.q: Which compound gives only one mononitro product with concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄?
questions.x: In 1,4-dimethylbenzene all four ring hydrogens are equivalent, so only one product forms. 1,2-Dimethylbenzene has two kinds of ring H (positions 3 and 4), 1,3-dimethylbenzene three (2, 4 and 5), and methylbenzene three (ortho, meta, para).

questions.q: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₃H₆Cl₂?
questions.x: On a three-carbon chain the two Cl atoms can be at 1,1 (CHCl₂CH₂CH₃), 1,2, 1,3 and 2,2 (CH₃CCl₂CH₃): four isomers. Missing a geminal isomer (both Cl on one carbon) gives 3; counting 2,3 or 3,3 separately repeats 1,2 and 1,1.

questions.q: In methoxymethane, CH₃OCH₃, the C–O–C bond angle is about:
questions.x: Oxygen is sp³ hybridised with two lone pairs, so the angle is near tetrahedral; the two bulky methyl groups push it slightly wider than in water, to about 110°. 104.5° is the H–O–H angle in water.

questions.q: Ozonolysis of an alkene, followed by zinc and water, gives butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, as the only organic product. The alkene is:
questions.x: Joining two butanone carbonyl carbons with C=C gives CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, 3,4-dimethylhex-3-ene. Hex-3-ene gives propanal, 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene gives propanone, and 3-methylpent-2-ene gives butanone plus ethanal.

questions.q: How many esters have the molecular formula C₄H₈O₂?
questions.x: Methanoates: HCOOCH₂CH₂CH₃ and HCOOCH(CH₃)₂; ethanoate: CH₃COOCH₂CH₃; propanoate: CH₃CH₂COOCH₃; that is 4. Missing the branched methanoate gives 3, and counting the two acids C₃H₇COOH as well gives 6.

questions.q: Apart from glycine, the α-amino acids that make up natural proteins are almost all:
o: Racemic mixtures of D- and L-isomers
questions.x: Every α-amino acid except glycine has a chiral α-carbon, and living things build proteins from the L-form only. Choosing a racemic mixture comes from thinking of laboratory synthesis, which does give both forms.

questions.q: Covalent cross-links that help hold the tertiary structure of many proteins are disulfide (–S–S–) bridges. They form between the side chains of:
questions.x: Cysteine has a –CH₂SH side chain, and two –SH groups are oxidised to an –S–S– bridge. Lysine side chains take part in ionic attractions, not covalent S–S links; glycine and alanine have no sulphur.

questions.q: Thermosetting plastics cannot be melted down and remoulded for recycling, unlike polythene. The reason is that thermosetting plastics:
o: Have only weak van der Waals forces between their chains
Have a three-dimensional network of covalent cross-links between chains
questions.x: Heating cannot break the covalent cross-links without decomposing the material, so it chars instead of melting. Thermoplastics such as polythene have separate chains held by weak intermolecular forces that heat overcomes, so the weak-forces option describes the opposite type.

questions.q: Which gas in the atmosphere is NOT a greenhouse gas?
questions.x: A greenhouse gas must absorb infrared radiation, which needs a vibration that changes the dipole of the molecule; N₂ has two identical atoms and does not absorb IR. N₂O looks like nitrogen but is a strong greenhouse gas, which makes it the tempting wrong choice.

questions.q: In a machine instruction such as ADD R1, R2, the part ADD that tells the CPU which operation to perform is called the:
questions.x: The opcode names the operation, here addition. R1 and R2 are the operands: the data or registers the operation works on.

questions.q: A weather office records 500 temperature readings and works out "Average this week: 31 °C". Later, the weekly averages of a whole year are used to draw a yearly chart. Which statement is correct?
o: The weekly average is data only, because it is a number
The 500 readings are information, because they were measured carefully
The yearly chart is data, because it was made from averages
The weekly average is information, and it becomes data for making the yearly chart
questions.x: Processed, meaningful results are information, but information from one process can be the data (input) of the next, as the weekly averages are for the yearly chart. A value is not data just because it is a number; what matters is whether it has been processed into a useful result.

questions.q: Using Boolean search operators, which pages match the query `cricket OR hockey`?
o: Pages containing cricket, hockey or both
Only pages containing both cricket and hockey
Pages containing cricket but not hockey
questions.x: OR widens the search: a page matches if it contains at least one of the words. Requiring both words is what AND does.

questions.q: Which wireless technology is commonly used to connect a mobile phone to wireless earphones a few metres away?
questions.x: Bluetooth uses short-range radio waves to link nearby devices such as phones and earphones. Satellite and microwave links are for long distances, and coaxial cable is not wireless at all.

questions.q: A router decides where to send each arriving packet by looking up the destination address in its:
o: List of MAC addresses on one port
questions.x: A router keeps a routing table of networks and the best next hop to reach each one. A list of MAC addresses per port is what a switch keeps, not a router.

questions.q: When Ali logs in, the system checks his username and password to confirm that he really is Ali. This step is called:
questions.x: Authentication proves who a user is, for example with a password. Authorisation comes after it and decides what the logged-in user is allowed to do.

questions.q: A program secretly gathers information about a user's activities, such as the websites she visits, and sends it to someone else without her knowledge. This program is:
questions.x: Spyware is malware that secretly collects information about the user and passes it on. A firewall and antivirus are protection tools, and freeware is simply software that is free to use.

questions.q: Using virtualisation, a company replaces 10 lightly used physical servers with virtual machines on 2 powerful servers. What is the main benefit?
o: Each virtual machine needs its own building
Less hardware, electricity and space are needed
The programs no longer need an operating system
The company no longer needs any network
questions.x: Combining many virtual machines on fewer physical servers (server consolidation) saves hardware, power and space. Each virtual machine still runs its own operating system.

questions.q: A data set has 1 000 labelled images. 80% of them are used to train a model and the rest to test it. How many images are used for testing?
questions.x: 80% of 1 000 is 800 for training, so 1 000 − 800 = 200 remain for testing. 800 is the training set, not the test set.

questions.q: Address labels are printed by mail merge, one label for each of 50 records. Each label sheet holds 14 labels. How many sheets are needed?
questions.x: 3 sheets hold 3 × 14 = 42 labels, leaving 8 labels, so a 4th sheet is needed (50 ÷ 14 = 3 remainder 8). Answering 3 ignores the 8 labels left over.

questions.q: In File Explorer, the document `notes.docx` is dragged with the mouse, with no key held down, from a folder on drive C: to a folder on a USB drive E:. What happens?
o: It is moved, and nothing stays on C:
Only a shortcut to it is made on E:
It is copied, and the original stays on C:
It is deleted and sent to the Recycle Bin
questions.x: Dragging a file to a different drive copies it by default, while dragging it within the same drive moves it. So `notes.docx` is now on both C: and E:.

questions.q: What is the main aim of normalisation?
o: To give every table as many columns as possible
To reduce redundancy and avoid insertion, update and deletion anomalies
To store the same data in several tables for safety
To sort every table by its primary key
questions.x: Normalisation splits tables so that each fact is stored once, which removes the anomalies caused by repeated data. Storing data in several places is the redundancy it tries to remove.

questions.q: In Student(RollNo, Name, City), records are often searched and sorted by City, which is not unique. What kind of key is City?
questions.x: A secondary key is a field used to search or sort records that need not be unique. Candidate and alternate keys must be unique, and City is not.

questions.q: A Remarks field will hold a teacher's comments, often several paragraphs and more than 255 characters long. Which data type should it have?
questions.x: Long Text (Memo) holds long passages of text. Short Text is limited to 255 characters, so longer comments would be cut off.

questions.q: Which Access query shows summarised values in a grid, with the values of one field as row headings and the values of another field as column headings?
questions.x: A crosstab query summarises data (for example sums or counts) in a row-and-column layout like a spreadsheet. A parameter query asks the user for a value when it runs.
347 / 10 = 34 with integer division, and 34 % 10 = 4, the tens digit; 347 % 10 = 7, the units digit. Stopping at n / 10 gives 34.
The digit characters have consecutive codes ('0' is 48, '7' is 55), so '7' - '0' = 7 and d * 2 = 14. Doubling the code of '7' itself gives 110.

questions.q: Which escape sequence moves the cursor to the next tab stop?
questions.x: \t is the horizontal tab. \n is a new line, \b a backspace and \a an alert (beep).
c holds the character '7', which lies between '0' and '9', so the second test is true and digit is printed. The first test fails because '7' is not between 'a' and 'z'.
n changes 6 -> 3 -> 10 -> 5 -> 16 -> 8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1, and c counts each change: 8. The starting value 6 is not a change, so 9 counts one too many.

questions.q: Which is a main advantage of dividing a C program into functions?
o: The same code can be called many times instead of being written again
The program no longer needs a `main()` function
Variables no longer need to be declared
The program is always free of errors
questions.x: A function is written once and called wherever it is needed, which saves repeated code and makes the program easier to test and change. Every C program still needs main(), and functions do not remove errors by themselves.

questions.q:
What happens when this Python program is run?
```
print("start")
x = 5
    y = x + 1
print(y)
```
o: start is printed, then an error is reported at line 3
Nothing is printed; Python reports an IndentationError, a syntax error, before running any line
questions.x: Python checks the syntax of the whole file before running it, and line 3 is indented for no reason, so an IndentationError (a kind of syntax error) is reported and not even line 1 runs. Printing start first is what would happen with a runtime error.
14 > 10 is True, so the inner `if` runs; 14 % 2 is 0, not 1, so its `else` prints Q. The outer `else` (R) is skipped because its condition was True.

questions.q:
How many lines of output does this statement print?
```
print("Lahore\nKarachi\nQuetta")
```
questions.x: Each `\n` is a newline escape sequence, so the text breaks after Lahore and after Karachi: three lines. The `\n` is not printed as two characters on one line.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
p = 1
for i in range(2, 7, 2):
    p *= i
print(p)
```
questions.x: `range(2, 7, 2)` gives 2, 4, 6, so p = 1 × 2 × 4 × 6 = 48. 720 multiplies every number from 2 to 6, ignoring the step; 12 is the sum 2 + 4 + 6.

questions.q: Which Tkinter widget is used only to show a piece of text, such as a heading, that the user can neither edit nor click?
questions.x: A Label just displays text (or an image). Entry and Text are boxes the user types into, and a Button is meant to be clicked.

questions.q: An undirected graph has vertices P, Q, R, S and edges P–Q, Q–R, R–S, S–P and P–R. What is the sum of the degrees of all its vertices?
questions.x: Degrees: P 3, Q 2, R 3, S 2, total 10. Every edge touches two vertices, so the sum is always twice the number of edges (2 × 5); 5 is the number of edges itself.

questions.q: In a tree, what is the node that has no parent called?
questions.x: The root is the top node and the only one with no parent. A leaf is a node with no children.

questions.q: In an experiment on a revision app, students are put into the app group or the no-app group at random, for example by drawing names. Why is this done?
o: So the app group always gets the stronger students
So the two groups are alike, and a difference in scores can be put down to the app
So that no control group is needed
So the results can be found without collecting data
questions.x: Random assignment spreads students' abilities evenly between the groups, so the only planned difference is the app. Choosing stronger students for one group would bias the result.

questions.q: In design thinking, what happens in the Define stage?
o: The users' main problem is stated clearly as a problem statement
A simple, early model of the solution is built
Users try the solution and give feedback
questions.x: After Empathize, the Define stage turns what was learnt about users into a clear statement of their problem. Brainstorming solutions is Ideate, building a model is Prototype and user feedback is Test.

questions.q: Which title best suits the passage?
o: How Telescopes Make Stars Look Larger
Two Ways to Tell Planets from Stars
Why the Air Above Us Never Rests
How the Ancients Named the Stars
questions.x: The passage gives the twinkling test and "a second test" of slow movement, then says "together they let anyone ... tell a world from a sun". Telescopes do not make stars larger: a star "appears as a single point of light" even through one.

questions.q: Why, according to the passage, does a planet usually shine steadily?
o: Its light does not have to pass through the air
It is larger than any of the stars
It gives off a steady light of its own
The bending of light from the many points of its disc averages out
questions.x: The planet is "a tiny disc, made of countless points of light" and "the bends average out across the disc". Its light is still bent by the air: "Each point is bent by the air".

questions.q: The passage suggests that a star seen through a large telescope would most likely:
o: still twinkle, because it would still appear as a single point
appear as a disc and stop twinkling
move against the other stars within a few weeks
shine more steadily than a planet does
questions.x: A star "even through a large telescope ... appears as a single point of light", and it is the narrow single beam that makes it twinkle. Appearing as a disc is what a planet does, not a star.

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the phrase "naked eye" refers to looking:
o: without a telescope or other aid
with an eye that has no protection from light
questions.x: The planet "looks like a dot to the naked eye" but is "really a tiny disc", in contrast to looking "through a large telescope". The phrase means the unaided eye.

questions.q: In the third paragraph, the words "this very habit" refer to:
o: a planet's slow change of position against the stars
the twinkling of stars near the horizon
the stars keeping their patterns from year to year
the steady glow of a planet
questions.x: The sentence before says "a planet slowly changes its position against the background of stars", and the name "meaning wanderer, records this very habit". The stars keeping their patterns is the background, not the wandering.

questions.q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Team games are better than individual sports for every child
Team and individual sports teach different lessons, so the choice should suit the child
Individual sports are too harsh for children to enjoy
Parents should let children change sports often
questions.x: The passage says the two kinds "teach different lessons" and ends "Wise parents therefore look less at the sport and more at the child". Neither kind is said to be better for every child.

questions.q: According to the passage, what is one drawback of team games?
o: Players are blamed personally for every defeat
A quiet child may take little part and never find out what he or she can do
Players are rarely helped by their teammates
Winners cannot share the credit with others
questions.x: "A quiet child can hide in a team, touching the ball rarely and never quite discovering what he or she can do". Personal blame for failure is a feature of individual sports, not team games.

questions.q: It can be inferred that, in the writer's view, the chance to hide that a team offers is:
o: a serious fault that makes team games useless
both a comfort for some children and a limit on others
an advantage with no real drawback
something found only in football and hockey
questions.x: The second paragraph treats hiding as a disadvantage, yet the last says "A shy child might flourish when carried along by a team". It is not a fault that makes team games useless, since they teach "a lesson in belonging".

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "glamorous" most nearly means:
o: attractive and likely to win attention
questions.x: A role "that may not be glamorous" is one that brings little attention, like defending while others score. "Fashionably dressed" is the word's common meaning, but the sentence is about a role, not clothes.

questions.q: How does the last paragraph relate to the second and third paragraphs?
o: It draws practical advice from the comparison they set out
It gives a new example of an individual sport
It contradicts what they say about team games
It repeats their points without adding anything
questions.x: The second and third paragraphs compare the two kinds of sport; the last begins "Wise parents therefore" and turns the comparison into advice about the child. It agrees with them rather than contradicting them.
